summary:
SensorScope is an explainable Earth observation harmonization platform developed to reconcile multi-decadal active-fire records between NASA's MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) sensors.Because MODIS and VIIRS differ in spatial resolution, overpass timing, and detection sensitivity, comparing raw hotspot counts across sensor transition periods risks confusing instrument sensitivity with real-world changes in burning. SensorScope addresses this challenge through an auditable, multi-model calibration pipeline (Global RMA and Context-Aware OLS) paired with an evidence-based Reliability Gate. Crucially, the system abstains from generating unsupported corrections and flags uncertainty whenever local observational evidence is sparse.
This platform is critical for climate science, wildfire management, and carbon accounting: it prevents artificial sensitivity jumps from distorting long-term emission baselines. Validated on real NASA FIRMS Standard Processing data across the Indo-Gangetic plain, SensorScope reduces held-out Fire Radiative Power (FRP) MAE by 15.3% with 94.6% empirical error coverage. SensorScope bridges 24 years of Earth observations with transparent, open-source science.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

SensorScope is an explainable satellite active-fire comparison and calibration platform focused on Punjab and Haryana, India. It uses NASA FIRMS Standard Processing observations from MODIS (Terra and Aqua, nominal 1 km resolution) and Suomi-NPP VIIRS (nominal 375 m resolution).

The sensors differ in spatial resolution, observation timing and detection characteristics. Therefore, their reported hotspot counts and Fire Radiative Power (FRP) cannot be treated as directly interchangeable.

SensorScope processes the data through four stages:

  1. Data ingestion and spatial aggregation: Reads NASA FIRMS CSV observations, validates and normalizes their fields, and aggregates sensor-specific hotspot counts and summed FRP into regular 0.1° geographic cell, date and day/night groups.
  2. Disagreement Atlas: Compares MODIS and VIIRS reporting patterns using hotspot-count differences, FRP differences, day/night analysis and spatial-temporal candidate associations. Candidate associations are not treated as confirmed physical fire matches.
  3. Calibration Engine: Compares three approaches: Model A (raw VIIRS identity baseline), Model B (global Reduced Major Axis regression), and Model C (context-aware Ordinary Least Squares regression). Model C uses predictor-side VIIRS FRP, VIIRS hotspot count and day/night status to estimate FRP on a MODIS reference scale.
  4. Reliability Gate: Evaluates sample support, validation bias, temporal subgroup behaviour and input-domain conditions. It assigns Green, Yellow or Red status and can abstain from applying a correction when the evidence is insufficient or unsupported. Raw sensor observations remain available.

The platform presents these results through five interactive sections: Overview, Disagreement Atlas, Calibration Lab, Fire Activity Calendar, and Methodology & Evidence.

What benefits does it have?

  • More careful cross-sensor comparisons: Helps researchers distinguish differences in satellite reporting from changes that might reflect actual fire activity.
  • Empirical calibration: On the 1,242-observation November 2023 comparative-evaluation cohort, Model C reduced FRP Mean Absolute Error from 30.93 MW to 26.19 MW, an improvement of approximately 15.3% over the raw VIIRS baseline.
  • Transparent uncertainty: A descriptive empirical error envelope contained 1,175 of 1,242 comparative-evaluation observations (94.6%). This is empirical coverage, not a guaranteed prediction interval.
  • Non-destructive analysis: Preserves raw sensor observations alongside calibrated estimates and communicates when corrections are not supported.
  • Reproducibility: Includes documented data processing, model comparisons and 10 automated tests.

The strict calibration cohort contains 2,554 co-active cell/date/day-night observations: 1,312 used for 2022 training and 1,242 for 2023 comparative evaluation. These are aggregated co-active observations, not confirmed individual fire matches.

What is the intended impact of the project?

SensorScope aims to support more responsible interpretation of satellite active-fire records. It can help researchers, environmental analysts and fire-monitoring teams investigate differences between satellite instruments before comparing observations across sensor transitions.

Its evidence-based approach is relevant to long-term fire monitoring, climate research and environmental reporting. However, the current system does not independently measure burned area, ground-truth fire events or greenhouse-gas emissions. It provides an auditable framework for comparing satellite observations and estimating FRP on a reference scale.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming language: Python 3.11+
  • Web application: Streamlit
  • Data processing: Pandas and NumPy
  • Statistical modelling: Scikit-learn (Ordinary Least Squares regression) and SciPy (Reduced Major Axis regression)
  • Interactive visualization: Plotly
  • Testing: Pytest, with 10 automated tests
  • Data source: NASA FIRMS Standard Processing, using MODIS Collection 6.1 and Suomi-NPP VIIRS Collection 2 active-fire observations
  • Version control: Git and GitHub
  • Deployment: Streamlit Community Cloud

How is your project creative?

SensorScope combines cross-sensor discrepancy analysis with an evidence-based Reliability Gate. Instead of automatically applying a mathematical correction to every observation, it checks whether the available evidence supports that correction.

Its Green, Yellow and Red states communicate different levels of evidence and caution. The system can abstain when the available sample is sparse, validation behaviour is unsuitable or input observations fall outside supported conditions.

The calibration models are interpretable statistical models rather than a black-box generative AI system. Their inputs, fitted coefficients, evaluation metrics and limitations are exposed for inspection.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Spatial resolution: MODIS and VIIRS have different nominal pixel sizes and detection characteristics, which can influence hotspot reporting.
  • Observation timing: Satellite overpass differences can allow fires to change between observations. Candidate associations therefore use explicit spatial and temporal thresholds.
  • Spatial aggregation: A regular 0.1° geographic grid provides a common reporting unit, but it is not an equal-area grid.
  • Observation limitations: Missing hotspot records do not necessarily indicate the absence of fire; cloud cover, satellite coverage and detection limitations can affect observations.
  • Model reliability: We separated the 2022 training cohort from the 2023 comparative-evaluation cohort and used date-grouped cross-validation within training data to examine model behaviour.
  • Scientific transparency: We retain raw observations, distinguish candidate associations from confirmed matches, report uncertainty and avoid applying corrections outside supported conditions.
